strengths: Ctrl-Z Sampling presents an intuitive inference-time strategy: detect reward stagnation, explore randomized rollback trajectories, and adaptively increase inversion depth when shallow exploration fails.

The method is training-free and potentially useful with existing conditional diffusion pipelines. Adaptive search depth is a meaningful distinction from fixed-depth resampling and path-search baselines.

Results on 500 Pick-a-Pic prompts and 200 DrawBench prompts consistently improve all four reported metrics over DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP. Improvements on HPSv2, PickScore, and AES provide some evidence beyond the ImageReward objective used during search.

The ablations examine reward-model choice, exploration triggering, inversion depth, and acceptance threshold. The comparison among always-on, random, and reward-triggered exploration usefully illustrates the quality–computation trade-off.
The paper is generally readable, and its overview figure, algorithm, tables, and qualitative comparisons communicate the main idea effectively.
weaknesses: The central hill-climbing/local-maximum interpretation is asserted rather than established. DDIM denoising does not optimize the reward model, and a decrease or plateau in rewards of intermediate clean estimates does not demonstrate that the trajectory has reached a local maximum. No landscape, trajectory, or escape-rate analysis validates this explanation.

The experimental support is too narrow for the broad claims of model agnosticism and universal applicability: evaluation uses only Stable Diffusion 2.1, DDIM, text-to-image generation, and two relatively small prompt sets. Results on another model family, sampler, or task are needed.

Evaluation is heavily coupled to the search objective. ImageReward guides the main method and is also the metric showing by far the largest gains. Improvements on independent metrics are much smaller, and there is no human preference study, statistical uncertainty, or significance analysis to establish that these differences are reliable rather than reward over-optimization.

The efficiency case is not fully convincing. A 7.6× NFE increase is substantial rather than clearly moderate, no wall-clock or memory measurements are reported, and SOP is compared at approximately 10× rather than under a strictly matched compute budget. Quality-versus-NFE curves would be more informative than one operating point.

The algorithm and prose contain consequential ambiguities. Algorithm 1 activates exploration when t <= T-lambda, which appears opposite to the stated restriction to the first lambda denoising steps. Moreover, d_max is said to be infinite by default, yet the algorithm supplies neither a global candidate budget nor a bound ensuring t+Delta remains within the diffusion schedule; N candidates per depth does not by itself guarantee termination.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the main-run batch size N_b is unspecified, the number of generated samples per prompt and seed protocol are unclear, baseline hyperparameters are largely omitted, and average NFEs are reported without their distribution. No code or supplementary implementation details are provided in the manuscript.

The qualitative evidence contains only four hand-selected prompts and no failure cases. The paper also lacks a substantive discussion of dependence on imperfect reward models, possible loss of diversity, reward hacking, and cases where repeated rollback degrades generation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving text-to-image alignment at inference time without retraining the diffusion model.

The proposed combination of reward-triggered exploration, stochastic rollback, and adaptive rollback depth is intuitive and potentially useful. The algorithm is reasonably easy to integrate with DDIM-style sampling.

The evaluation includes two prompt sets, four automatic metrics, several relevant sampling baselines, qualitative examples, and ablations over reward models, exploration triggers, thresholds, and rollback depths.
The paper acknowledges inference cost and reports function-evaluation overhead, with Ctrl-Z using fewer evaluations than the configured SOP baseline.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is vulnerable to reward over-optimization. ImageReward both guides the search and supplies the metric showing the largest gains. The remaining metrics are correlated learned preference models, and there is no human evaluation or held-out reward model specifically designed to test generalization beyond this optimization signal.

The improvements over SOP on non-optimized metrics are very small: on Pick-a-Pic, the HPSv2, AES, and PickScore gains are only 0.0007, 0.010, and 0.017, respectively. No multiple-run variance, confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or per-prompt win rates are reported, so it is unclear whether these differences are reliable. The much larger ImageReward improvement does not resolve the circular-evaluation concern.

The algorithm and prose contain serious inconsistencies. With timesteps descending from T to 1, Algorithm 1 enables exploration when t <= T-lambda, whereas the text says exploration is restricted to the first lambda denoising steps. The default d_max is declared unbounded, yet the paper says that a finite candidate budget N per depth guarantees termination; it does not, and sufficiently large Delta would make t+Delta exceed the valid schedule. Candidate variables and clean-image estimates also carry inconsistent timestep superscripts. These issues prevent an unambiguous implementation of the claimed default method.

The experimental scope is too narrow for the broad claims of model agnosticism and general applicability: only Stable Diffusion 2.1 with DDIM, one CFG setting, 700 total prompts, and one GPU configuration are tested. There is no validation on a modern diffusion/flow model, another sampler, higher resolution, or a different conditional-generation task.

The comparison to inference-time search is incomplete. Several closely related particle, dynamic-search, beam-search, and evolutionary-search methods are cited but not evaluated; calling them orthogonal is not convincing because they address the same quality-versus-test-time-compute setting. A matched-NFE quality curve is needed instead of one hand-configured SOP point. Moreover, 7.6x NFEs is substantial rather than clearly 'moderate,' and wall-clock latency and memory are not reported.

The novelty appears incremental relative to resampling, restart/zigzag sampling, and reward-guided path search: the principal addition is increasing rollback depth when shallow candidates fail. The hill-climbing/local-maxima interpretation is presented heuristically, without a defined objective landscape, theoretical result, or diagnostic evidence demonstrating that detected reward plateaus actually correspond to local maxima or that deeper rollback escapes them.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits sampling seeds and number of generated samples per prompt, precise benchmark subset construction, uncertainty estimates, implementation details for adapted baselines, the main-experiment batching parameter N_b, and an exact accounting of NFEs. No code or supplementary reproducibility material is identified.

The ablations do not isolate the adaptive-depth contribution under equal compute. In fact, exploring at every step performs substantially better than the proposed reward trigger, suggesting that much of the gain may come from additional best-of-many search. Comparisons against fixed rollback depths and fixed search procedures at matched average NFEs are necessary to establish the claimed advantage of adaptivity.

The qualitative evidence contains only four selected prompts with one output per method and no seed-selection protocol. It is therefore insufficient to support claims about consistent global coherence or semantic alignment. Overall, the method is plausible and has some merit, but ambiguities in the algorithm and insufficiently independent, statistically supported evaluation leave the scientific case below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper offers a simple and intuitive inference-time strategy: reward-triggered exploration with progressively deeper latent inversion when shallow perturbations fail. This adaptive search depth is a meaningful distinction from fixed-depth resampling and path-search baselines.

The method requires no diffusion-model training and is compatible in principle with pretrained conditional diffusion models. Algorithm 1 and the ablations provide a reasonably clear account of the trigger, acceptance threshold, search depth, and reward-model choices.

On both Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench, Ctrl-Z improves all four reported metrics over DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP. The gains over SOP are especially notable for the optimized ImageReward metric while using fewer average function evaluations (7.6x versus 10x).

The reward-model and exploration-trigger ablations are informative. They show that different rewards steer different qualities and clearly expose the quality-compute trade-off between always, random, and reward-based exploration.
The qualitative examples support the intended benefit on compositional prompts, particularly object inclusion and global semantic consistency.
weaknesses: The evaluation cannot yet establish that the gains reflect human-perceived quality rather than reward optimization. ImageReward both guides the search and supplies the metric with the largest gains; the remaining metrics are correlated learned preference models, and PickScore is trained on data related to Pick-a-Pic. A blinded human study or evaluation with a demonstrably independent reward would materially strengthen the case.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims of broad applicability: experiments use only Stable Diffusion 2.1 with DDIM, two small prompt sets totaling 700 prompts, and four qualitative examples. Results on a modern diffusion/flow model, another sampler or architecture, and harder compositional benchmarks are needed to support model-agnostic and general-quality claims.

Compute-controlled evidence is incomplete. A 7.6x NFE increase is substantial despite being described as moderate, wall-clock latency is not reported, and there is no quality-versus-NFE curve or equally budgeted best-of-N/reward-ranking baseline. Thus it is unclear how much benefit comes from adaptive rollback rather than simply evaluating many reward-selected candidates.

No uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed results, or significance tests are reported. Several improvements over SOP on non-optimized metrics are small—for example, HPSv2 improves only from 0.2671 to 0.2678 on Pick-a-Pic—so their reliability is difficult to assess.

The local-maxima/hill-climbing interpretation is heuristic: diffusion denoising does not explicitly optimize the reward, and the paper does not demonstrate that reward stagnation of intermediate clean estimates corresponds to a latent-space local optimum. The framing should therefore be presented as intuition rather than an established characterization.

Algorithmic specification has important ambiguities. The default dmax is described as unbounded, yet the pseudocode does not cap t+Delta at the maximum diffusion timestep, and a finite candidate budget per depth does not guarantee termination of an unbounded depth loop. The default batch size Nb, exact stopping behavior, runtime distribution, seeds, and implementation availability are also insufficiently documented for reliable reproduction.

Overall, the adaptive-depth idea and consistent results support a slight preference for acceptance, but the recommendation remains borderline because independent human validation, broader models, and strict compute-matched comparisons are missing.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, training-free, model-agnostic sampling strategy: reward-triggered exploration with progressively deeper inversion. Adaptive search depth is intuitive and potentially useful compared with fixed-depth resampling or search-over-path baselines.

The evaluation covers two distinct diffusion architectures, three prompt benchmarks, several alignment/aesthetic metrics, and compositional categories. The ablations examine search depth, candidate width, reward choice, exploration trigger, acceptance threshold, and exploration window.

Results consistently improve substantially over ordinary DDIM. T2I-CompBench shows particularly notable gains, such as SD2.1 shape accuracy increasing from 48.91 for SOP to 53.97 and spatial accuracy from 16.97 to 19.29.

The paper acknowledges reward over-optimization, fixed-threshold scheduling, diminishing returns, and limited large-budget evaluation. The presentation and qualitative comparisons are generally clear.
weaknesses: Equation (5) appears mathematically incorrect for a variance-preserving forward transition. Its noise coefficient is sqrt((1-alpha_{t+Delta})/alpha_t), whereas the conditional transition from x_t should ordinarily use sqrt(1-alpha_{t+Delta}/alpha_t). The stated operator therefore has variance 1/alpha_t rather than one. This central discrepancy makes the implemented method ambiguous and could substantially alter its behavior.

Algorithm 1 contains consequential inconsistencies: termination is attributed to the candidate budget even though depth controls termination; the text calls inversion depth unbounded despite taking d_max as input; and line 27 tests the last candidate's r_cand rather than best_score, so a qualifying earlier candidate may not stop the search. Code is not supplied to resolve these ambiguities.

Evidence for superiority over the strongest baseline is modest and mixed relative to the large cost. On SD2.1, Ctrl-Z versus SOP changes Pick-a-Pic HPSv2 by only +0.11 and AES by +0.005 while reducing PickScore by 0.10; on DrawBench it gains only 0.01 HPSv2 and loses 0.05 PickScore. Hunyuan-DiT results are similarly mixed. Yet the method requires roughly 7.7-8.8 times the base denoising evaluations.

The cost analysis reports normalized denoiser evaluations rather than wall-clock time, memory, or total computation. Repeated VAE decoding and reward-model scoring can be substantial, particularly at 1024 resolution, but are omitted. Describing a 7-9x denoising overhead as moderate or practical is therefore insufficiently supported.

The evaluation provides no human study, confidence intervals, repeated-seed variance, or significance tests. The number of samples per prompt and seed-matching/selection protocol are also unclear. This is important because many reported differences against SOP are very small, and the displayed qualitative examples have no stated selection procedure.

ImageReward is used both to guide search and as a headline evaluation metric, making the large ImageReward gains partly circular and vulnerable to reward hacking. Independent metrics help, but often show much smaller or inconsistent gains; no analysis verifies that deeper exploration improves human preference rather than exploiting learned evaluators.

The hill-climbing/local-maxima interpretation is heuristic rather than established: rewards of predicted clean images at different noise levels need not be calibrated or monotonically comparable, so a decrease does not demonstrate that the trajectory reached a local maximum. The novelty over reward-guided path search is correspondingly incremental—principally increasing rollback depth after failed candidates.

Baseline attribution is inconsistent: SOP is attributed to Ma et al. in the main paper but to Kim et al. in the supplement. Along with threshold inconsistencies in the supplementary text/caption, this weakens clarity and reproducibility. Overall, the idea has merit, but the central mathematical ambiguity and insufficiently controlled evidence slightly favor rejection in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving text-to-image diffusion outputs at inference time without retraining the generator.

The adaptive search-depth idea is intuitive and potentially useful. It combines reward-triggered exploration, multiple stochastic candidates, and progressively stronger inversion in a model-agnostic procedure.

Evaluation covers two substantially different architectures, Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT, and three prompt suites. The exploration-depth/width, reward-model, trigger, threshold, and exploration-window ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence.
The authors report computational cost through average NFEs and acknowledge reward overfitting, fixed-threshold scheduling, and limited scaling experiments.
weaknesses: Under the appropriate Algorithms/General contribution type, the empirical case is not convincing enough. Against the strongest baseline, SOP, most Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench improvements are extremely small or negative: for SD2.1, Ctrl-Z loses 0.10/0.05 PickScore while improving HPSv2 by only 0.11/0.01; for Hunyuan-DiT it loses AES on both datasets and slightly loses ImageReward on Pick-a-Pic. These results do not substantiate the repeated claim of substantial, broadly consistent improvement.

The method directly searches using ImageReward and is then evaluated mainly with learned preference/reward models, including ImageReward itself. Cross-metric evaluation only partly alleviates this circularity because the metrics are correlated learned proxies; PickScore also has close domain overlap with Pick-a-Pic. There is no human evaluation demonstrating that the reward increases correspond to perceptible improvements rather than reward-model exploitation.

No uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed results, statistical tests, or per-prompt paired analysis are reported. This is consequential given the stochastic search and the very small margins over SOP. The manuscript specifies benchmark prompt counts but not the number of generated samples or random seeds per prompt, and the qualitative examples lack a selection protocol.

The algorithm is internally inconsistent. Algorithm 1 terminates a depth search based on the last candidate's `rcand`, rather than the best candidate score; after a failed search it assigns `rprev = best_score` even when that score is below the previously accepted reward, contradicting the claimed non-decreasing acceptance rule. The clean-estimate indexing and candidate variables are also ambiguous. Moreover, the text claims that default inversion depth is unbounded and that N guarantees termination, whereas the implementation uses `dmax = 3`; N alone cannot guarantee termination of an unbounded depth loop.

The central hill-climbing/local-maximum interpretation is asserted rather than established. A reward drop between consecutive noisy clean-image estimates is neither a demonstrated local maximum nor necessarily stagnation, since estimate quality and reward calibration change systematically with diffusion time. No landscape analysis or controlled experiment validates the claimed mechanism of escaping broad or steep maxima.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. Ctrl-Z requires about 7.72x NFEs for SD2.1 and 8.79x for Hunyuan-DiT, plus repeated reward-model evaluations. Only denoiser NFEs are counted: wall-clock latency, reward-evaluation cost, batching assumptions, peak memory, and sequential depth-search overhead are omitted. Thus the claim that the method is practical for local inference or has minimal overhead is not supported.

Baseline coverage and attribution are unclear. The main text associates SOP with Ma et al. (2025), while the supplement describes it as Kim, Kim, and Park (2025). Several closely related 2025 inference-time search/scaling works are discussed but not evaluated, leaving uncertainty about comparison with the strongest relevant alternatives.

Reproducibility is limited despite reporting hardware and library versions: no code or pseudocode resolution of the algorithmic ambiguities is provided, and scheduler details, seed matching, sampling repetitions, exact benchmark protocol, and qualitative selection procedure are missing. Overall, the method has merit, but the combination of specification errors, potentially circular evaluation, absent statistical/human validation, and overstated efficiency makes the present scientific case favor rejection. strengths: The paper presents a simple, intuitive, training-free sampling strategy: reward stagnation triggers stochastic inversion, and the exploration depth increases when shallow perturbations fail. Adaptive depth is a meaningful distinction from fixed-depth resampling and search-over-path baselines.

The method is model-agnostic and is evaluated on both U-Net-based Stable Diffusion 2.1 and transformer-based Hunyuan-DiT, with generally consistent improvements across Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, and T2I-CompBench.

The empirical study is reasonably broad. It includes multiple alignment and aesthetic metrics, qualitative comparisons, two architectures, and ablations of exploration depth, candidate width, reward model, trigger policy, acceptance threshold, and exploration window.

Results support the central claim that deeper exploration can be more useful than merely widening a shallow search. Ctrl-Z notably improves compositional categories on T2I-CompBench and usually matches or exceeds SOP while using fewer average NFEs.

The paper is clearly motivated and visually well presented. The landscape analogy and sampling diagrams make the method easy to understand, while the supplementary material supplies useful implementation details and candidly discusses reward over-optimization and scaling limitations.

The submission fits the Algorithms/General contribution type: its value lies in a practical inference algorithm and its empirical quality-compute trade-off, rather than in a foundational account of diffusion as literal hill climbing.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies entirely on automated metrics and provides neither human evaluation nor uncertainty estimates, multiple-seed statistics, or significance tests. This is important because the numerical advantages over SOP are often small and sometimes mixed across metrics.

ImageReward is both the default search objective and an evaluation metric, making the large ImageReward gains partly expected. Results on HPSv2, PickScore, AES, and compositional metrics reduce this concern, but optimizing alternative rewards also produces corresponding metric-specific gains. Human judgments or evaluation with stronger independent models would better establish genuine perceptual improvement rather than reward exploitation.

Compute fairness is not fully convincing. Ctrl-Z averages 7.72x–8.79x the baseline NFEs, versus 9x for SOP, but exact matched-budget quality curves against SOP and random/always exploration are missing. Table 5 narrows this issue but still compares configurations with unequal NFEs. Thus the claimed exploration-efficiency advantage is promising rather than conclusive.

The absolute inference overhead is substantial despite being described as moderate. Practical evidence should include wall-clock time, memory, reward-model evaluation cost, parallel hardware assumptions, and latency—not only denoiser NFEs. The method may be unattractive for many local-inference scenarios at roughly 8x the standard sampling cost.

The hill-climbing/local-maximum interpretation is heuristic and is not theoretically established. Intermediate predicted-clean-image rewards can vary because prediction quality changes with noise level, so a reward decrease does not necessarily identify a local optimum in a common landscape. The paper should temper this framing or validate that the trigger meaningfully detects recoverable failures.

There are reproducibility and specification inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 tests the final candidate score rather than the best score when deciding whether to stop; the statement that an unbounded inversion depth terminates because N is finite is incorrect; the main experiment uses dmax=3 despite discussion of unbounded depth; and SOP is attributed inconsistently to Ma et al. in the main paper and Kim et al. in the supplement. Code availability and generation seeds are also unspecified.

Generality is demonstrated on two architectures but only within text-to-image DDIM-style sampling and relatively dated base models. Compatibility with modern flow-matching systems, alternative solvers, and stronger contemporary generators remains an unsupported claim. These concerns keep the recommendation borderline, although the method and current evidence are strong enough for a slight preference toward acceptance.
